issue.title: Data race between `sys._current_exceptions()` and a concurrently attaching thread

labels.name: type-bug
labels.description: An unexpected behavior, bug, or error

labels.name: extension-modules
labels.description: C modules in the Modules dir

issue.body:
### Bug description:

In the free-threaded build, `sys._current_exceptions()` iterates every thread state under stop-the-world + `HEAD_LOCK` and reads `t->thread_id`.

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/ecdef1773006529b0fea6639d0effeecbb41679c/Python/pystate.c#L2808-L2817

But a newly started thread sets `tstate->thread_id` in `bind_tstate()` without holding `HEAD_LOCK`. Its `PyThreadState` is already on the interpreter's thread list by this point.

https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/ecdef1773006529b0fea6639d0effeecbb41679c/Python/pystate.c#L164-L178

A thread that is still attaching is not yet stop-the-world-stoppable. `_PyEval_StopTheWorldAll()` therefore does not pause it, and its unlocked write to `tstate->thread_id` races the stop-the-world reader in `_PyThread_CurrentExceptions`.

Reproducer:
```python
import sys
import threading

stop = threading.Event()

def reader():                      # keep stop-the-world almost always active
    for _ in range(20000):
        sys._current_exceptions()

def churn():                       # continuously attach new threads (bind_tstate)
    for _ in range(20000):
        t = threading.Thread(target=lambda: None)
        t.start()
        t.join()

readers  = [threading.Thread(target=reader) for _ in range(8)]
churners = [threading.Thread(target=churn)  for _ in range(4)]
for t in readers + churners: t.start()
for t in readers + churners: t.join()
```

TSAN Report:
```
WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race (pid=94157)
  Read of size 8 at 0x0001081180b0 by thread T1:
    #0 _PyThread_CurrentExceptions pystate.c:2817
    #1 sys__current_exceptions sysmodule.c.h:1180
    #2 cfunction_vectorcall_NOARGS methodobject.c:508
    #3 PyObject_Vectorcall call.c:327
    #4 _Py_VectorCallInstrumentation_StackRefSteal ceval.c:768
    #5 _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault generated_cases.c.h:1906
...
  Previous write of size 8 by thread T9:
    #0 bind_tstate pystate.c:178
    #1 _PyThreadState_Bind pystate.c:2660
    #2 thread_run _threadmodule.c:384
    #3 pythread_wrapper thread_pthread.h:234

SUMMARY: ThreadSanitizer: data race pystate.c:2817 in _PyThread_CurrentExceptions
```


### CPython versions tested on:

CPython main branch

### Operating systems tested on:

macOS

<!-- gh-linked-prs -->
### Linked PRs
* gh-152755
* gh-156202
<!-- /gh-linked-prs -->

comments.body:
I took a closer look at this on the latest `main` (`564c58c718bc`) using a free-threaded Windows debug build.

I couldn't independently reproduce the reported ThreadSanitizer warning because TSAN isn't available with the Windows/MSVC free-threaded build, so I focused on tracing the implementation and verifying the reported code paths.

From what I found, the synchronization concern described in the report appears consistent with the current implementation.

`_PyThreadState_New()` publishes the new thread state into `interp->threads.head` while holding `HEAD_LOCK`, but the child thread later calls `_PyThreadState_Bind()`, where `bind_tstate()` initializes `tstate->thread_id` without `HEAD_LOCK`.

Meanwhile, `_PyThread_CurrentExceptions()` performs stop-the-world, acquires `HEAD_LOCK`, iterates the published thread-state list, and reads `t->thread_id`. Since `bind_tstate()` runs before `_PyThreadState_Attach()`, my understanding is that an attaching thread is not yet fully covered by stop-the-world, so the write to `thread_id` may race with those readers.

While tracing this path, I also noticed that `_PyThread_CurrentFrames()` and `PyThreadState_SetAsyncExc()` use the same `thread_id` publication/read pattern, so the discussion may extend beyond `_current_exceptions()` alone.

I also considered a few possible implementation approaches (synchronizing publication under `HEAD_LOCK`, atomic publication/access, or excluding published-but-unbound thread states from these APIs), but each seems to have different lifecycle implications, so I don't want to guess at the intended design.

Before attempting a PR, I'd appreciate some guidance from the runtime/free-threading maintainers on the intended invariant here.

Should published-but-not-yet-bound thread states be visible to APIs such as `_current_exceptions()` and `_current_frames()`, or is the expectation that `thread_id` publication itself should be synchronized (for example via `HEAD_LOCK` or atomic access)?

If there's a preferred direction, I'd be happy to investigate further and work on a patch.

Confirmed on a free-threaded ThreadSanitizer build (`--with-thread-sanitizer --disable-gil --with-pydebug`); the reproducer fires on essentially every run:

```
WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race
  Read  of size 8 ... _PyThread_CurrentExceptions  Python/pystate.c:2817
  Write of size 8 ... bind_tstate                  Python/pystate.c:178
```

`bind_tstate` writes `thread_id` after the `PyThreadState` is on `interp->threads.head` but before the thread attaches, so stop-the-world can't pause it and the store races `sys._current_exceptions()`. `_PyThread_CurrentFrames` reads the same field but I couldn't make it race — its `if (frame == NULL) continue;` gate means the thread only reaches the read after `PyEval_AcquireThread` has synchronized through `tstate->state`.

Suggested labels: `topic-free-threading`, `interpreter-core` (on top of `type-bug`).

Fix is small — store `thread_id`/`native_thread_id` with a relaxed atomic in `bind_tstate` and read them with a relaxed atomic load in the thread-list readers, matching `tstate->state`. Opened #152755 (TSan-clean across 30+ runs).
